# The In-Between

I've been thinking about liminal spaces lately. You know the ones—airport terminals at three in the morning, hospital waiting rooms with their particular fluorescent hum, that moment on a Sunday evening when the weekend has already ended but Monday hasn't quite begun. The spaces that don't quite belong to any recognizable moment of living.

There's something about these places that makes people honest. Or maybe just tired. I watched a woman at baggage claim yesterday stare at the carousel for five minutes without moving, and I realized she wasn't waiting for her suitcase. She was waiting for permission to go wherever she was going. The machine would tell her when it was time.

I used to think I knew who I was. That feels ridiculous to say now, but it's true. I had a job that fit me reasonably well, a apartment that faced the right direction, friends I'd known long enough to stop impressing. I had a routine that felt like identity. Then one day I woke up and felt like I was lying in someone else's bed, someone else's life, wearing someone else's skin. It was the strangest feeling—not painful exactly, more like realizing you've been holding your breath and you haven't even noticed.

Everyone says you have to reinvent yourself. That's the language now. *Reinvent*. Like you're a tech startup that failed its Series B. But what if you just want to slowly remember who you were before everyone else started defining you? What if reinvention is just paying attention again?

I've started walking differently. Not for exercise—I'm not that person. But I'll take these routes that have no destination, that loop back on themselves. I pass the same coffee shop four times and the barista is starting to recognize me, which means I'm either finally becoming a regular or I'm having some kind of breakdown. Probably both. She made my latte art into a small heart yesterday and didn't comment on it, which felt like grace.

My mother called and I couldn't bring myself to answer. She wanted to know if I was eating properly, if I was dating, if I'd gotten the promotion yet. Questions that all meant: are you still on the track we agreed upon? And I realized that no, I'm not, and I'm not sure I want to be. But how do you tell your mother that the life she helped you build no longer fits without making her feel like she did something wrong? You don't, probably. You just stop answering calls for a while.

There's this thing that happens when you read too much—you start thinking in other people's sentences. I caught myself yesterday framing my anxiety in the language of Didion, my loneliness in the vocabulary of Plath. It's as if I can't even feel things without first finding someone else who's felt them more eloquently. Which either means everything's been done before, or that we're all fundamentally alone in our experiences and literature just makes us feel less so. Maybe it's both.

I watched a documentary about deep sea creatures—animals that live in the crushing darkness where sunlight never reaches. They've developed their own light, these creatures. Bioluminescence. They glow for each other in the dark. And it struck me that maybe that's what we're all doing. Creating little lights in the spaces where we can't see. Writing things down. Telling stories. Reaching toward other people.

The world is very loud right now. I'm sure you've noticed. Everyone has opinions and they're sharing them constantly, in capital letters, with evidence and counterevidence and receipts. And I just keep thinking about my grandmother who lived through actual difficult things and rarely spoke about them. She would say sometimes, "Well, there's nothing to be done about it now," and move on to asking if you wanted more potatoes. There was something powerful in that. Not repression exactly—more like an understanding that not every feeling required an audience.

I've been relearning how to be bored. That sounds like a joke, but it's not. Boredom is almost extinct now. We've automated it away, scheduled it out of existence. But boredom is where thinking happens. Boredom is the soil where actual thoughts can grow, not the recycled thoughts we scroll past, not the opinions we've inherited. Just—nothing happening. The mind left to its own devices. It's terrifying and wonderful.

Sometimes I think about parallel versions of myself. The one who answered the phone when Mom called. The one who went for the promotion. The one who's still with the person I dated five years ago. The one who moved to that other city. And I wonder if those versions of me are wondering about this version, the one writing to strangers at midnight about liminal spaces and bioluminescent creatures and the unbearable weight of choosing who to become.

But here's what I've figured out: I think those versions aren't separate. I think they're all just me, existing in superposition, and the act of paying attention to one sort of collapses the others. Maybe that's what growing up is. Not becoming someone new, but collapsing the possibilities down into one actual life, and learning to be okay with all the versions you'll never get to be.

The airport terminal is still humming. Planes are still taking off. People are still waiting for permission to move on to the next thing. And I'm still here in the in-between, which, it turns out, is where most of us live most of the time. We just usually don't notice.

Maybe that's enough. Maybe paying attention is the whole thing.
